meaning: Strongly denies a feeling or evaluation: "not ... at all," "not the least bit ...".
connection: i-adjective く-form + もなんともない

senses.label: No feeling at all
senses.meaning: Denies a feeling such as pain, fear or sadness. Much stronger than plain 「〜くない」. Often sounds tough or nonchalant.
senses.connection: 痛く・怖く・悲しく・寂しく + もなんともない
examples: A scratch like this doesn't hurt one bit.
Living alone isn't lonely at all.
Even being dumped by a guy like that didn't make me the least bit sad.

senses.label: Nothing special
senses.meaning: Denies an evaluation such as interesting, rare or impressive. What others find remarkable is nothing to the speaker. The tone is cold and can sound dismissive.
senses.connection: 面白く・珍しく・すごく・うらやましく + もなんともない
examples: That kind of story isn't interesting at all.
Around here, snow is nothing unusual at all.

notes: Very harsh and dismissive. Saying 「うれしくもなんともない」 or 「面白くもなんともない」 about a gift or recommendation will deeply hurt the giver; never use it with a boss or client. To politely say you're not interested, use 「あまり興味がなくて」.
An i-adjective must be in its く-form before 「も」: ✕「痛いもなんともない」→ ○「痛くもなんともない」. Nouns and な-adjectives cannot attach directly: ✕「好きもなんともない」→ ○「好きでもなんでもない」.
It differs only slightly from 「なんとも言えない」 but means something quite different: 「なんとも言えない味」 is "an indescribable taste" (usually praise), whereas 「おいしくもなんともない」 means "not tasty at all".
Often used to save face or act tough: 「怖くもなんともない」 can in many contexts hint that the speaker is in fact a little scared, so judge by tone.

daily.title: Acting tough
daily.description: A child who fell down tells their parents they're fine.
daily.example: I'm fine. It doesn't hurt one bit.

daily.title: Asked about a breakup
daily.description: Playing it cool when a friend is worried.
daily.example: I'm not sad at all, so don't worry.

daily.title: Reviewing a movie
daily.description: Complaining to a friend after the film.
daily.example: That movie wasn't scary at all.

work.title: Judging a proposal
work.description: A coworker privately comments on a rival's proposal.
work.example: Honestly, that proposal is nothing new at all.

etymology: 「なんとも」 is 「何と」 + 「も」, originally "however you put it." With a negative, 「なんともない」 means "nothing is wrong." Adding 「〜くも」 in front denies the adjective completely.
formation: It is built from two parts: 「i-adjective く-form + も」 and 「なんともない」. The く-form is the adjective's continuative form and can take the topic particle 「も」 directly; 「なんとも」 is 「何と」 ("how to put it") + 「も」, and with 「ない」 it becomes "nothing worth mentioning". So 「痛くもなんともない」 literally says "it's not painful, nor anything else for that matter", wiping out the feeling and every other possibility, which makes the denial far more thorough than 「痛くない」. This "neither A nor B" pattern of total negation is emotional in itself, hence the scornful or tough-guy tone. Nouns and な-adjectives must first borrow the copula 「で」 to take 「も」, giving the matching form 「でもなんでもない」.

similar.title: 〜でもなんでもない
similar.explanation: A sister form with the same origin and meaning. 「でもなんでもない」 follows nouns and な-adjectives (「友達でもなんでもない」「好きでもなんでもない」); 「もなんともない」 follows the く-form of i-adjectives (「痛くもなんともない」). Both are emotional, total denials.

similar.title: ちっとも〜ない
similar.explanation: Both mean "not at all". 「ちっとも」 is an adverb that can modify many predicates (「ちっとも来ない」); 「〜もなんともない」 only denies feelings and evaluations, with a more scornful or tough tone.

similar.title: まったく〜ない
similar.explanation: 「まったく〜ない」 is an objective, complete negation, usable in writing and speech and fine in formal settings; 「〜もなんともない」 is spoken, strongly emotional, and unsuitable for formal situations.

meaning: Says a situation (usually a problem or flaw) is not limited to one case but is found widely.
connection: noun + に限ったことではない

senses.label: Not just ...
senses.meaning: Points out that a problem is not unique to that subject; it exists elsewhere too. Mostly for negative things. Common in commentary and the news.
senses.connection: noun + に限ったことではない／に限ったことではなく
examples: The falling birthrate is not just Japan's problem.
His being late is nothing new; it didn't start today.
This problem isn't limited to young people; it's a problem for all of society.

senses.label: Casual forms
senses.meaning: In speech, people often say 「〜に限ったことじゃない」 or 「〜に限った話じゃない」. Same meaning, more casual.
senses.connection: noun + に限ったことじゃない／に限った話じゃない
examples: High prices aren't just a Tokyo thing.
We're not the only company that's busy.

notes: It points in the opposite direction from 「〜に限って」: 「うちの子に限って」 means "my child, of all kids (wouldn't)", stressing exclusivity, while 「うちの子に限ったことではない」 means "it's not just my child", stressing generality. Mixing them up reverses the meaning.
You cannot swap the particle for 「とは」: 「日本人とは限らない」 means "not necessarily Japanese", while 「日本人に限ったことではない」 means "it's not only Japanese people".
Saying 「君の遅刻は今日に限ったことじゃない」 implies the person is always like this. It dredges up past faults and sounds heavy-handed, so don't use it with a boss or client.
Only a noun can come before it: ✕「遅刻するに限ったことではない」→ ○「遅刻は彼に限ったことではない」.

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: A wife tells a friend her husband always leaves things lying around.
daily.example: My husband being sloppy isn't anything new.

daily.title: Talking about the news
daily.description: Friends discuss rising housing costs.
daily.example: Rents going up isn't just happening in this city.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentator analyzes labor shortages.
work.example: Labor shortages are not limited to the nursing-care industry.

work.title: Internal meeting
work.description: A manager says the whole company must deal with a problem.
work.example: The high number of errors is not limited to this department; it's a company-wide issue.

etymology: 「限る」 means "to limit, to be restricted to." 「に限ったこと」 is "a matter limited to ...," and with 「ではない」 it means "not limited to ...".
formation: It combines 「に」 (the range or target of the limit), the た-form 「限った」 of 「限る」 (to limit), the formal noun 「こと」, and the negative 「ではない」. The 「た」 here marks a state, not the past, so 「限ったこと」 means "a matter confined to N". The whole phrase literally means "it is not a matter limited to N": what is denied is the limiting itself, so the sense becomes "it exists beyond N too". Because it is often used to rebut the view that "this is a problem unique to one place", it mostly appears with problems and faults, expressing a judgment that they are widespread.

similar.title: 〜に限らず
similar.explanation: Same origin (both from 「限る」) and a similar meaning. 「に限らず」 is a mid-sentence connector, "not only ... (but also ...)", and can be positive or negative (「子供に限らず大人も楽しめる」); 「に限ったことではない」 usually closes the sentence as a judgment, often about how widespread a negative phenomenon is.

similar.title: 〜のみならず
similar.explanation: Similar: both mean "not limited to ...". 「のみならず」 is a formal, written connector followed by "but also ..."; this pattern rebuts the idea that "only here is there a problem" and usually ends the sentence as a conclusion.

similar.title: 〜に限って
similar.explanation: Same origin but opposite direction: 「に限って」 stresses "of all things, only" (「急いでいる時に限って電車が遅れる」), whereas this pattern stresses "not only, it's everywhere".

similar.title: 〜とは限らない
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「とは限らない」 is a partial negation, "not necessarily ..." (「高い物がいい物とは限らない」); this pattern denies being limited to a given target, meaning "the scope is wider".

meaning: "Once it's in someone's hands" or "when up against someone": anything gets handled easily, or nobody stands a chance.
connection: noun (usually a person) + にかかったら／にかかっては／にかかると／にかかれば

senses.label: In their hands, anything is easy
senses.meaning: Praises someone's great skill: even hard tasks are easy for them. Usually followed by something being solved easily. Often paired with 「どんな〜も」.
senses.connection: person + にかかったら／にかかれば + どんな〜も…
examples: In his hands, even the hardest problem gets solved right away.
In the hands of a great doctor, an illness like this would soon be cured.

senses.label: No match for them
senses.meaning: Nobody can stand up to this person. The tone is half resigned, half admiring. 「〜にかかっては」 is mostly used this way.
senses.connection: person + にかかっては／にかかると + かなわない／形無しだ etc.
examples: When it comes to that kid, even her strict father is no match.
With my mom, no excuse ever works.

notes: What goes before 「に」 is the "handler" (a person), and what follows says how things get handled; reverse them and it makes no sense: ✕「この問題にかかったら、彼はすぐ解決する」→ ○「彼にかかったら、この問題もすぐ解決する」.
It looks like 「〜にかかっている」 but differs greatly: 「成功は君にかかっている」 means "success depends on you", not "once it's in your hands, it will succeed".
The 「かかる」 in 「医者にかかる」「病気にかかる」「罠にかかる」 is an ordinary verb (see a doctor, catch an illness, fall into a trap): 「医者にかかったら治った」 means "I saw a doctor and got better", and is not this grammar point.

The second sense of 「〜にかかっては」 carries a teasing "there's no beating him" tone, mostly used of children, family and acquaintances; saying 「部長にかかってはかなわない」 about a boss or elder may be taken as calling them difficult, so use it with care.

daily.title: Praising a friend
daily.description: Praising a friend who is good at fixing things.
daily.example: Leave it to Tanaka, and even a broken computer gets fixed in no time.

daily.title: Talking about your child
daily.description: A parent tells a friend their child is great at sweet-talking.
daily.example: When it comes to our daughter, even my husband turns completely soft.

daily.title: Talking about family
daily.description: Chatting about mom's cooking.
daily.example: In my mom's hands, even leftovers become a feast.

work.title: Introducing a coworker
work.description: Introducing the company's expert to a client.
work.example: In her hands, even the most complex data can be organized quickly.

work.title: After negotiations
work.description: A coworker sighs about a tough client.
work.example: Up against that director, there's no way our terms will get through.

etymology: 「かかる」 can mean "to fall into someone's hands, to be dealt with by someone," as in 「敵の手にかかる」. From this came the conditional use "once it's in someone's hands."
formation: The verb 「かかる」 has the sense of "falling into someone's hands and being dealt with" (「敵の手にかかる」「名医の手にかかる」), and 「に」 marks the handler. Add a conditional 「たら／ば／と」 and you get "if it's put in someone's hands", which naturally leads to the result for the thing being handled: in capable hands, anything is resolved with ease. With 「ては」, since 「〜ては」 itself often introduces unfavorable or helpless outcomes (as in 「そんなに食べては太る」), the sense tilts toward "nobody can handle him". So the first part must be a person (or personified handler) and the second the outcome for the thing.

similar.title: 〜をもってすれば／〜をもってしても
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning: both are "if one uses ... (one can do it)". 「をもってすれば」 is more formal, usually preceded by ability, skill or power (「彼の技術をもってすれば」); 「にかかったら」 is more colloquial and usually follows a person.

similar.title: 〜にかけては
similar.explanation: Both praise someone's ability and are often compared. 「にかけては」 follows a field: "when it comes to ... (nobody beats him)"; 「にかかったら」 follows a person and says what happens once things reach their hands.

similar.title: 〜にかかっている
similar.explanation: Same origin, both from the verb 「かかる」. 「にかかっている」 means "depends on ..." and goes at the end of a sentence to name the key factor; 「にかかったら」 means "if it falls into ...'s hands", a hypothetical followed by a result.

meaning: Deliberately putting on an air of something; acting like or posing as. Negative.
connection: noun / な-adjective stem / i-adjective stem + ぶる

senses.label: Pretending to be ...
senses.meaning: Pretending to be something you are not. Usually critical or annoyed. Common: 「学者ぶる」「上品ぶる」「大人ぶる」.
senses.connection: noun / な-adjective stem + ぶる／ぶって／ぶった + noun
examples: He acts like a scholar and uses nothing but difficult words.
That affectedly refined way of talking gets on my nerves.
You're just a junior high student. Stop acting like a grown-up.

senses.label: Putting on airs
senses.meaning: After stems like 「偉い」 or 「悪い」, it means putting on airs or striking a pose. 「偉ぶる」 is acting important; 「悪ぶる」 is acting bad.
senses.connection: 偉 + ぶる, 悪 + ぶる, いい子 + ぶる
examples: After a small promotion, he started acting all important.
She only plays the good girl in front of the teacher.
He's the company president, but he doesn't put on airs at all.

senses.label: Keeping someone in suspense
senses.meaning: 「もったいぶる」 is a set phrase: to be coy, to make a big deal of something, to keep people waiting.
senses.connection: もったいぶる／もったいぶって／もったいぶらないで
examples: Stop teasing and just tell me already.

notes: It differs by one sound from 「〜びる」 but praise and criticism flip: 「大人びる」 means naturally looking mature (it can be a compliment), while 「大人ぶる」 means deliberately acting grown-up (a criticism). To praise a child's maturity say 「大人びている」; 「大人ぶっている」 turns it into a jab.

It is inherently negative. Telling someone 「偉ぶっている」 or 「上品ぶっている」 to their face directly calls them phony and is very rude to a boss or client. Conversely, the negative 「偉ぶらない人」 is a common compliment (someone with no airs).
It cannot follow verbs: ✕「知るぶる」→ ○「知っているふりをする」. I-adjectives take the stem without 「い」: ✕「偉いぶる」→ ○「偉ぶる」.
The 「ぶる」 in 「かぶる」「揺さぶる」「目をつぶる」 is just part of the verb and is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Criticizing a friend
daily.description: Complaining that a friend was showing off at a party.
daily.example: That guy acted like a connoisseur and talked about nothing but wine.

daily.title: Hurrying someone
daily.description: A friend says they have good news but won't share it.
daily.example: Quit stalling and just say it.

daily.title: Talking about your kid
daily.description: A mother says her child behaves well only in front of others.
daily.example: My kid always plays the good child in front of other people.

work.title: Talking about a boss
work.description: A subordinate praises a modest boss.
work.example: Our manager has a great track record, but he never acts superior.

work.title: Discussing a new hire
work.description: Coworkers talk privately about a newcomer.
work.example: He's just a new hire, but he acts like a senior. It's a real problem.

etymology: 「ぶる」 is a suffix generally thought to share its origin with 「振る（ふる）」, meaning "to act or behave in a certain way." Later it came to mean deliberately putting on an act.
formation: 「ぶる」 is a suffix, generally thought to share its origin with 「振る」 and 「振る舞う」, meaning "to put on the behavior of ..."; it attaches to noun or adjective stems and becomes voiced 「ぶる」. 「学者ぶる」 literally means "to act the part of a scholar". Putting something on is an active, intentional act rather than natural, which gives it the sense of "pretending, putting on a show" and hence a negative tone. Since the whole thing is a godan verb, it conjugates freely (「ぶって」「ぶった + noun」「ぶらない」), and the negative 「偉ぶらない」 means "not putting on airs".

similar.title: 〜ふりをする
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning: both are "pretend". 「ふりをする」 is neutral pretending and can follow verb clauses (「寝たふりをする」); 「ぶる」 follows only nouns or stems and criticizes putting on airs.

similar.title: 〜びる
similar.explanation: Both mean "to look like ..." and are often compared. 「大人びる」 and 「古びる」 describe a look that arises naturally and are fairly neutral; 「大人ぶる」 is a look put on deliberately, and negative.

similar.title: 〜じみる
similar.explanation: Similar, and both carry a negative evaluation. 「子供じみる」 is childishness showing without the person realizing; 「ぶる」 is deliberately putting on a certain image.

meaning: Having the look or tendency of something; "-ish," "like a ...". Mostly negative.
connection: noun + じみる／じみた + noun／じみて

senses.label: Like a ...
senses.meaning: Someone's words or actions seem like those of a certain kind of person, not fitting their age or position. Usually critical. Most common: 「子供じみた」「年寄りじみた」.
senses.connection: 子供・年寄り・所帯 etc. + じみた + noun／じみている
examples: You're a grown adult. Stop doing such childish things.
She's young, but her way of thinking is like an old person's.
Since getting married, she's become totally domestic and frumpy.

senses.label: Smacking of ...
senses.meaning: Something has a certain (usually bad) quality, such as theatrical, crazy or preachy. Common: 「芝居じみた」「狂気じみた」「説教じみた」.
senses.connection: 芝居・狂気・説教・脅迫 etc. + じみた + noun
examples: His theatrical apology showed no sincerity.
That plan is downright insane.
I'm sick of preachy talks.

notes: It is almost always negative and can't be used to praise: to praise a mature child, ✕「大人じみた子」→ ○「大人びた子」.

Calling someone's behavior 「子供じみた真似」 or saying 「所帯じみた」 is criticism. In particular 「所帯じみる」 describes someone steeped in household drudgery and drained of glamour, which is quite rude to say of another person (especially a woman).
Use 「じみた」 before a noun and 「じみている」 as a predicate: ✕「子供じみる行動」→ ○「子供じみた行動」.
「汗じみたシャツ」 has the literal meaning "a shirt soaked with sweat", not "a shirt like sweat".

daily.title: Criticizing a partner
daily.description: A girlfriend is fed up with her boyfriend's sulky behavior.
daily.example: Cut out those childish little tricks.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's exaggerated gesture.
daily.example: The man spread his arms with a theatrical gesture.

daily.title: Chatting with a friend
daily.description: Commenting on how a friend has changed.
daily.example: Lately you've started talking like an old man.

work.title: After a meeting
work.description: Coworkers talk about the boss's lecture.
work.example: The manager's preachy pep talk went on for a whole hour.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report describes an unusual demand.
work.example: A business partner sent an email that bordered on a threat.

etymology: 「じみる」 is generally thought to come from 「染みる（しみる）」, "to soak in, to stain." From "becoming stained with a color or smell," it came to mean "taking on a certain look or habit."
formation: 「じみる」 is generally thought to come from 「染みる」 (to soak in, to be stained), voiced after a noun. 「Noun + じみる」 literally means "soaked through with N, tinged with the flavor of N". Soaking in happens unnoticed, from the inside out, so it expresses "unwittingly taking on the look of N" rather than putting it on deliberately. What soaks in is often something unwanted like sweat or grease stains, so when applied to people and matters it also tends to be a negative judgment. As an ichidan verb, it uses 「じみている」 for a resulting state and 「じみた」 before a noun.

similar.title: 〜めく
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning: both are "to have the look of ...". 「めく」 is often neutral (「春めく」「謎めいた」); 「じみる」 almost always carries a negative tinge.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: Similar. 「っぽい」 is colloquial, combines freely and can be positive or negative; 「じみる」 is more literary, with limited collocations, and is mostly criticism.

similar.title: 〜びる
similar.explanation: Both mean "to look like ...". 「大人びる」 and 「古びる」 are neutral or even positive; 「子供じみる」 and 「年寄りじみる」 mostly carry criticism.

meaning: "Together with all of ...," "the whole ..."; stresses that an entire group takes part.

senses.label: The whole group together
senses.meaning: An entire group takes part as one. Usually neutral or positive. Common: 「家族ぐるみ」「町ぐるみ」「地域ぐるみ」.
senses.connection: 家族・町・地域・学校 + ぐるみの + noun／ぐるみで
examples: Our family and the family next door are close friends.
The whole town got ready to welcome tourists.
The whole community watches over the children.

senses.label: Organized wrongdoing
senses.meaning: Used for misconduct: not one person, but the whole organization was involved. Common in the news: 「組織ぐるみ」「会社ぐるみ」.
senses.connection: 組織・会社・社 + ぐるみの + 不正／犯罪／隠蔽
examples: This fraud was carried out by the organization as a whole.
A company-wide cover-up has come to light.

senses.label: Along with everything
senses.meaning: The original meaning: together with the wrapping. Today it mainly survives in 「身ぐるみ」, "everything you have on you."
senses.connection: set phrases such as 身ぐるみ剥がされる
examples: I was robbed of everything I had while traveling.

notes: It follows only nouns for groups or wholes, never individuals: ✕「私ぐるみ」「田中さんぐるみ」→ ○「家族ぐるみ」「町ぐるみ」.

「組織ぐるみ」 and 「会社ぐるみ」 immediately suggest organized wrongdoing or a cover-up. For positive all-hands activities, 「会社を挙げて」 or 「全社で」 is more natural; saying 「御社ぐるみで〜」 to a partner comes close to an accusation, so avoid it.
「ぬいぐるみ」 and 「着ぐるみ」 are independent nouns unrelated to this pattern; 「身ぐるみ剥がされる」 means "to be stripped of everything", not "the whole body together".

daily.title: Talking about neighbors
daily.description: Telling a friend you get along well with your neighbors.
daily.example: Our whole family is close with the Yamadas.

daily.title: Community events
daily.description: A local explains the town festival.
daily.example: This festival is a big event for the whole town.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: Hearing about a corporate scandal.
daily.example: I can't believe the whole company was hiding it.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on falsified company data.
work.example: It has been revealed that the inspection data was falsified at an organizational level.

work.title: Local government document
work.description: Describing disaster-prevention efforts.
work.example: We will promote community-wide disaster-prevention activities.

etymology: 「ぐるみ」 comes from 「くるみ」, the stem form of 「くるむ」 (to wrap), voiced after a noun. It first meant "wrapping and all," and then "the whole, everyone."
formation: 「ぐるみ」 comes from the continuative form 「くるみ」 of the verb 「くるむ」 (to wrap up), voiced after a noun. 「Noun + ぐるみ」 literally means "wrapping all of N together", i.e., "along with the wrapping, the whole lot". In 「身ぐるみ」 it keeps this original sense, "along with everything on one's body"; with group nouns such as 「家族」「町」「組織」 it means "wrapping everyone in the group together" → "everyone takes part". Because it stresses that no one is left out, used of improper conduct it carries the accusation that "the whole organization is complicit". It is nominal: 「ぐるみの」 before a noun, 「ぐるみで」 as an adverb.

similar.title: 〜ずくめ
similar.explanation: Both carry a sense of "all" and are often memorized together. 「ずくめ」 means the content is uniform (「黒ずくめ」「いいことずくめ」); 「ぐるみ」 means a group takes part as a whole (「町ぐるみ」).

similar.title: 〜とともに
similar.explanation: Both can mean "together". 「とともに」 means "with someone", the two sides on equal footing (「家族とともに暮らす」); 「家族ぐるみ」 means "the whole family as one", stressing that the entire group is involved.

meaning: Being absorbed in something and doing it to your heart's content; also, indulging without restraint.

senses.label: Enjoying to the full
senses.meaning: Being immersed in something you love. Usually positive. Common: 「読書三昧」「ゴルフ三昧」「温泉三昧」.
senses.connection: 読書・釣り・ゴルフ・温泉 etc. + 三昧の + 日々／生活
examples: Since retiring, I spend my days reading to my heart's content.
I relaxed over the long weekend, soaking in hot springs to my heart's content.
I spent the whole summer vacation playing video games.

senses.label: Unrestrained indulgence
senses.meaning: After words like 「贅沢」, 「わがまま」 or 「放蕩」, it means doing as one pleases without limits. Negative.
senses.connection: 贅沢・わがまま・放蕩 + 三昧
examples: He lives a life of total luxury on his parents' money.
As an only child, he grew up getting his way in everything.

notes: The reading is voiced 「ざんまい」: ○「読書三昧」 (「どくしょざんまい」); it is read 「さんまい」 only as a standalone noun.
「贅沢三昧」「わがまま三昧」「遊び三昧」 criticize someone's indulgence. Telling someone about their retirement 「遊び三昧ですね」 may sound like sarcasm about idling; better to say 「趣味を満喫されていますね」.
It follows only nouns, not verbs: ✕「食べる三昧」「読む三昧」→ ○「グルメ三昧」「読書三昧」. For "eat as much as you like" use 「食べ放題」, not 「三昧」.

daily.title: Talking about a vacation
daily.description: Telling a coworker how you spent your time off.
daily.example: I spent my whole vacation fishing.

daily.title: Retirement plans
daily.description: A father talks about his plans after retiring.
daily.example: When I retire, I want to play golf every day.

daily.title: Reading gossip
daily.description: Reading about a rich heir.
daily.example: Apparently he's just partying all the time on his parents' inheritance.

work.title: Travel ad
work.description: A travel agency's tagline.
work.example: Enjoy a hot-spring holiday in a room with its own open-air bath.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on misused public money.
work.example: The former chairman is suspected of living lavishly on public funds.

etymology: 「三昧」 is a Buddhist term, a transliteration of Sanskrit samādhi: a state where the mind is fully focused on one point. It came to mean "devoting yourself to something," and then "doing something as much as you like."
formation: 「三昧」 is a Buddhist term transliterating Sanskrit samādhi, a state of the mind concentrated on one thing without distraction, and it is voiced to 「ざんまい」 after a noun. 「Noun + 三昧」 literally means "mind fully absorbed in N", so it expresses "being wholly immersed in N, enjoying N to the full". When N is itself a behavior like 「贅沢」 or 「わがまま」, being fully immersed in luxury or selfishness means "without restraint", which produces the negative tone. Since the whole is a noun, it takes 「の」 before a noun, 「だ」 as a predicate and 「に」 as an adverb.

similar.title: 〜放題
similar.explanation: Similar: both can mean "to one's heart's content". 「放題」 follows the verb ます-stem and stresses "no limits" (「食べ放題」); 「三昧」 follows a noun and stresses "being absorbed in it" (「読書三昧」).

similar.title: 〜てばかりいる
similar.explanation: Both can mean "doing nothing but ...". 「てばかりいる」 usually carries dissatisfaction or blame (「遊んでばかりいる」); 「三昧」 is normally an enjoying tone, and critical only with words like 「贅沢」 or 「わがまま」.

similar.title: 〜ばかり（nothing but）
similar.explanation: 「Noun + ばかり」 means "nothing but ...", applies to anything and often carries dissatisfaction; 「三昧」 is used only for a person immersed in some activity or way of life.

meaning: After a noun: "involving, tied up with ...," often money or politics. After an age: "about ... years old."
connection: noun + がらみ（の）／number (age) + がらみ

senses.label: Tied up with ...
senses.meaning: Closely connected to or entangled in something. Usually money, politics, elections or incidents, often complicated or negative. Common in the news.
senses.connection: 金・政治・選挙・事件・仕事 + がらみの + noun／がらみで
examples: I got dragged into a money-related dispute.
Rumor has it that these personnel changes are tied to the election.
I'm busy even on weekends with work-related socializing.

senses.label: About ... years old
senses.meaning: After an age, it means "roughly ... years old." Mostly for middle-aged people and a bit old-fashioned. Common: 「四十がらみの男」.
senses.connection: ages like 四十・五十 + がらみの + person
examples: A man of about forty came into the shop.
A gentleman of about fifty asked me for directions.

notes: 「金がらみ」 and 「政治がらみ」 hint at tangled interests and murky dealings, a suspicious way of putting it. Asking someone 「〇〇さんとは金がらみの関係ですか」 is nearly an accusation and very rude; to say neutrally "related to ...", use 「〜に関する」 or 「〜関係の」.

The age usage applies only to adults (typically in their forties or fifties) as a rough age, mostly in fiction and reports describing strangers: ✕「十がらみの子供」. Calling someone 「四十がらみの方」 to their face sounds like sizing up their age and is impolite.
After a number it means age, not "related to that number": 「五十がらみの男」 is "a man around fifty".
「しがらみ」 (ties, shackles) is an independent noun and not part of this grammar point.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: Seeing a report on a political scandal.
daily.example: Another politics-related scandal?

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A mystery novel describes a suspect.
daily.example: The culprit was a thin man of about fifty.

daily.title: Warning a friend
daily.description: Advising a friend not to lend money to acquaintances.
daily.example: Even with friends, you should be careful with anything involving money.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on a bribery case.
work.example: Prosecutors are investigating it as a corruption case tied to public works projects.

work.title: Explaining weekend plans
work.description: Telling a coworker about work socializing on the weekend.
work.example: I've got a round of golf with a client this weekend.

etymology: 「がらみ」 comes from 「からみ」, the stem form of 「絡む（からむ）」 (to entangle), voiced after a noun. It first meant "entangled, involved." The age use is generally thought to come from "hovering around that number."
formation: 「がらみ」 comes from the continuative form 「からみ」 of the verb 「絡む」 (to entangle), voiced after a noun. 「Noun + がらみ」 literally means "entangled with N", and entanglement itself implies complexity and difficulty shaking free, so it is often used for money, politics, elections and other tangled interests, with a flavor of "something going on behind the scenes". After an age number, it is generally thought to extend from "entwined around that number" to "around ... years old". The whole is nominal: 「がらみの」 before a noun.

similar.title: 〜にまつわる
similar.explanation: Similar: both mean "related to ...". 「にまつわる」 is often used for legends, stories and memories (「城にまつわる伝説」) and is neutral; 「がらみ」 is often used for money, politics and other interests, hinting at inside circumstances.

similar.title: 〜にかかわる
similar.explanation: Similar. 「にかかわる」 means "affects (a serious matter)" (「命にかかわる」) and is neutral; 「がらみ」 stresses being entangled in a complicated or dubious relationship.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい
similar.explanation: Corresponds to the age sense: both mean "about". 「くらい」 works with any quantity and is the most common; 「がらみ」 is used only for adult ages and sounds old-fashioned.

meaning: "Nothing but ...," "full of ..."; usually for good or lavish things.

senses.label: Nothing but ...
senses.meaning: Being surrounded by one kind of thing, usually good or plentiful. Common: 「いいことづくし」「ごちそうづくし」「カニづくし」.
senses.connection: noun + づくしの + noun／づくしだ
examples: This year was full of good things.
Dinner at the inn was crab, crab and more crab.
New Year's was one feast after another, so I put on a little weight.

senses.label: A collection of ...
senses.meaning: Listing or gathering things of one kind one after another. Often used in titles, show names and product names.
senses.connection: noun + づくし (e.g. 「花づくし」「名所づくし」)
examples: The kimono's pattern features flowers from every season.

notes: Its keynote is "abundant, complete", mostly used for good things and fine food; with scars or mistakes it sounds unnatural: ✕「傷づくしの車」→ ○「傷だらけの車」.
It is not entirely the same as 「ずくめ」: for being dressed all in one color only 「黒ずくめ」 works, ✕「黒づくし」; 「いいことづくし」 and 「いいことずくめ」 are both fine.
「お心尽くしの料理」 praises the host's "thoughtfully prepared dishes" and does not mean "all heart"; on receiving hospitality, 「お心尽くしをありがとうございます」 is very fitting.

daily.title: Talking about a trip
daily.description: Telling a friend about the food on a trip.
daily.example: In Hokkaido, it was seafood, seafood, seafood every day.

daily.title: Catching up
daily.description: A friend shares their recent good luck.
daily.example: Lately I won the lottery and got promoted. It's been nothing but good news.

work.title: Restaurant menu
work.description: A Japanese restaurant offers a seasonal set menu.
work.example: We have prepared a course featuring the flavors of autumn.

work.title: Introducing a new product
work.description: A marketer explains a new plan's benefits.
work.example: This plan has discounts and perks. It's all advantages.

etymology: 「づくし」 comes from 「つくし」, the stem form of 「尽くす（つくす）」 (to exhaust), voiced after a noun. It first meant "using everything up, listing them all," and then "all ...".
formation: 「づくし」 comes from the continuative form 「つくし」 of the verb 「尽くす」 (to exhaust, to use up completely), voiced to 「づくし」 after a noun, which is why the kana is 「づ」. 「Noun + づくし」 literally means "using up all of N, laying it all out", so it expresses "nothing but N, N in full supply". Laying everything out suggests completeness and abundance, so it is mostly used for fine food and good things, and also for titles collecting a category of things (「花づくし」「名所づくし」). It is nominal: 「づくしの」 before a noun, 「づくしだ」 as a predicate.

similar.title: 〜ずくめ
similar.explanation: The closest in meaning: both mean "all ...". 「ずくめ」 works for good and bad, and for colors and clothing (「黒ずくめ」); 「づくし」 is mostly for abundant good things and also has an "enumerating one by one" use (「花づくし」).

similar.title: 〜だらけ
similar.explanation: Both mean "full of ...". 「だらけ」 is mostly negative (「ミスだらけ」「傷だらけ」); 「づくし」 is mostly positive.

similar.title: 〜まみれ
similar.explanation: Both mean "covered with ...". 「まみれ」 means a surface covered in liquid or filth (「泥まみれ」) and is negative; 「づくし」 doesn't mean covering, it describes richness of content.

meaning: "Smacking of ...," "with a whiff of ..."; mostly for unpleasant words or actions.
connection: noun / verb ます-stem + がましい

senses.label: Smacking of ...
senses.meaning: Words or actions seem to be doing something that makes others uncomfortable. Negative. Common: 「恩着せがましい」「押し付けがましい」「言い訳がましい」.
senses.connection: 恩着せ・押し付け・言い訳・未練 + がましい／がましく
examples: I wish you'd stop talking like I owe you something.
This may sound like an excuse, but please let me explain the situation.
I called my ex, still unable to let go.

senses.label: Presumptuous
senses.meaning: 「差し出がましい」 is a set phrase meaning "meddlesome, presumptuous." Often used humbly before giving an opinion.
senses.connection: 差し出がましいようですが／差し出がましいことを申しますが
examples: Forgive me for being presumptuous, but may I say something?

senses.label: Grand and glorious
senses.meaning: 「晴れがましい」 is a rare positive example: "grand, glorious, honored." Common for ceremonies and award events.
senses.connection: 晴れがましい + 舞台／場
examples: I'm honored to stand on such a grand stage.

notes: 「差し出がましいようですが」 is a modest opener that can be used to give opinions to a superior, but using 「がましい」 to evaluate the other person is an accusation: telling a boss 「部長の言い方は押し付けがましいです」 is very rude.
Collocations are essentially fixed and you can't coin new ones: ✕「説明がましい」→ ○「言い訳がましい」; ✕「親切がましい」→ ○「恩着せがましい」.
「晴れがましい」 is a positive exception (grand, glorious); don't read it as "putting on airs" just because 「がましい」 is mostly negative.
It is unrelated to 「〜ほうがましだ」: 「まし」 means "somewhat better", whereas 「がましい」 is an adjectival suffix.

daily.title: Complaining about a relative
daily.description: Complaining to a friend about how a relative talks.
daily.example: My aunt is always pushing her advice on me.

daily.title: After getting help
daily.description: A friend keeps bringing up a favor, which is annoying.
daily.example: It's nice that they helped, but they act like I owe them.

work.title: Making a suggestion to a boss
work.description: A subordinate politely raises a concern in a meeting.
work.example: Forgive me for overstepping, but I have some concerns about this plan.

work.title: Award ceremony
work.description: A winner gives an acceptance speech.
work.example: Thank you for inviting me to such a grand occasion.

etymology: 「がましい」 is a suffix generally thought to come from old suffixes like 「かまし」 meaning "looking like ...". Added to a noun or verb stem, it forms an adjective meaning "seeming to ..., with an air of ...".
formation: 「がましい」 is a suffix that attaches to a noun or verb ます-stem to form an i-adjective, generally thought to come from the old suffix 「かまし」, meaning "looking like ..., having the air of ...". 「Noun + がましい」 means "seeming to be doing N": it isn't said outright, but the intention shows in words and actions, so 「恩着せがましい」 means "sounding as if one is doing a favor". What shows through is mostly an off-putting intent such as doing favors, imposing or making excuses, so the whole leans negative; 「晴れがましい」 is one of the few positive exceptions. As an i-adjective it conjugates to 「がましく」「がましさ」.

similar.title: 〜じみる
similar.explanation: Similar: both mean "having the look of ..." with criticism. 「じみる」 says the whole comes across like a certain kind of person or thing (「子供じみた」); 「がましい」 focuses on an unpleasant intention showing in words and actions (「恩着せがましい」).

similar.title: 〜めく
similar.explanation: Both mean "having the feel of ...". 「めく」 can be neutral (「春めく」); 「がましい」 describes almost exclusively objectionable words and actions.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: Similar: both mean "-like". 「っぽい」 is colloquial, combines freely and can be positive or negative; 「がましい」 has fixed collocations and mostly describes attitude or manner of speaking.

meaning: "Looking like ..., similar to ... (but not the real thing)"; mostly for shady practices or fakes.

senses.label: Bordering on ...
senses.meaning: Not quite the thing in form, but practically the same as some improper act. Strongly critical. Common: 「詐欺まがい」「脅迫まがい」.
senses.connection: 詐欺・脅迫・恐喝・ヤクザ + まがいの + noun
examples: Sales tactics bordering on fraud and targeting the elderly are increasing.
He sent me a letter that was practically a threat.
I'm being harassed by gangster-like debt collectors.

senses.label: Imitation
senses.meaning: Something made to imitate the real thing: a fake or knockoff. The noun 「まがい物」 means "a fake."
senses.connection: 本物・ブランド + まがいの + noun／まがい物
examples: Fake brand goods that look just like the real thing are going around.
I got stuck with a fake at a street stall.

notes: It carries a strong accusing tone: calling someone's approach 「詐欺まがいだ」 says "it's close to fraud", and using it with a client or partner can cause serious disputes.
「まがい」 means "like but not" and is not a verdict: the news says 「詐欺まがいの商法」 precisely because it may not legally count as fraud. Don't treat it as a synonym of 「詐欺だ」.
It is the exact opposite of 「紛う方なき」 (「まごうかたなき」): 「紛う方なき本物」 means "unmistakably the real thing", whereas 「本物まがい」 means "a fake that passes for genuine".

daily.title: Warning family
daily.description: Adult children warn their elderly parents about door-to-door sales.
daily.example: There are a lot of scammy door-to-door salespeople lately, so be careful.

daily.title: After online shopping
daily.description: Complaining to a friend about buying a fake.
daily.example: The bag I bought online was a knockoff.

work.title: Consumer alert
work.description: A consumer center issues a warning.
work.example: Please beware of tactics bordering on fraudulent sales, such as aggressive solicitation.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on improper marketing.
work.example: The company is said to have attracted customers with ads bordering on fraud.

etymology: 「まがい」 comes from the stem form of 「紛う（まがう）」, "to be confused with, hard to tell apart." So 「〜まがい」 means "hard to tell from ..., just like ...".
formation: 「まがい」 comes from the continuative form of the verb 「紛う」 (「まがう」, to be mistaken for, to be hard to tell apart), nominalized and placed after a noun. 「Noun + まがい」 literally means "something hard to tell from N", i.e., "looks like N but isn't quite N". The "hard to tell apart" goes two ways: bad conduct that "can't be told from fraud or extortion" → close to ...; fakes that "can't be told from the real thing" → imitations. The core is "like but not", so the speaker both reserves that it's not strictly N and passes negative judgment. It is nominal: 「まがいの」 before a noun, and it also forms the noun 「まがい物」.

similar.title: 〜も同然だ
similar.explanation: Similar: both mean "practically the same as ...". 「も同然だ」 is the speaker's judgment "as good as" and works for good or bad (「勝ったも同然だ」); 「まがい」 is mostly for improper conduct and imitations, stressing "like but not".

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: Both can mean "like ...". 「っぽい」 is colloquial and can be positive or negative; 「まがい」 is mostly for illegal acts, fraud and fakes, with a clearly negative tone.

similar.title: 〜めく
similar.explanation: Both mean "having the look of ...". 「めく」 is mostly neutral (「春めく」); 「まがい」 stresses resembling something improper, with strong criticism.

meaning: After a few words such as 「柄」, 「いつ」 and 「心」: different from one's usual or true self, "unusually, out of character."
connection: 柄／いつ／心 + にもなく（にもない）

senses.label: Unusually
senses.meaning: 「いつにもなく」 means different from usual: "unusually, for once." 「いつになく」 is also common.
senses.connection: いつにもなく／いつになく + adjective / verb
examples: He was unusually quiet today.
He came to me for advice with an unusually serious face.

senses.label: Out of character
senses.meaning: 「柄にもなく」 means doing something that doesn't fit your personality or position: "not like me/him." Often self-mocking.
senses.connection: 柄にもなく + 緊張する／照れる etc.
examples: It's not like me, but I got nervous.
Totally out of character, he showed up with a bouquet.

senses.label: Insincere
senses.meaning: 「心にもない」 means words that don't reflect your true feelings: "insincere, not meant." Common: 「心にもないことを言う」.
senses.connection: 心にもない + こと／お世辞
examples: I ended up saying something I didn't mean.

notes: 「心にもない」 and 「心ない」 differ only by 「にも」 but mean different things: 「心にもないことを言う」 is "to say something one doesn't mean", while 「心ない言葉」 is "cold, hurtful words".
Using 「柄にもなく」 about yourself is a natural self-deprecation; using it about a boss or elder (「部長、柄にもなく〜」) says they're "not behaving as befits their position" and is rude.
It is limited to a few fixed collocations and can't be extended by analogy: ✕「彼にもなく」「普段にもなく」→ ○「いつになく」「柄にもなく」; in 「年甲斐もなく」 no 「に」 goes in the middle.

daily.title: Talking about a friend
daily.description: Noticing a friend acting differently today.
daily.example: He's in an unusually good mood today.

daily.title: Poking fun at yourself
daily.description: Admitting to a friend that a movie made you cry.
daily.example: It's not like me, but I cried at the movie.

daily.title: After an argument
daily.description: Apologizing to the other person.
daily.example: I'm sorry I said things I didn't mean earlier.

work.title: In a meeting
work.description: A coworker notices a change in the boss.
work.example: The manager was speaking in an unusually strict tone.

work.title: Giving a speech
work.description: An honoree speaks modestly on stage.
work.example: I'm not used to this and I'm rather nervous, but allow me to say a few words.

etymology: 「柄（がら）」 means one's status or character, 「いつ」 means usual times, and 「心」 means one's true feelings. With 「にもない」, "not even in ...," it means "out of keeping with one's true self."
formation: It is built from a noun + 「に」 (range, location) + 「も」 (even) + 「ない」 (does not exist); 「Nにもない」 literally means "not found even within N". 「柄」 is a person's standing or character, so 「柄にもない」 means "(an act) not in one's character" → "out of character, unbefitting one's position"; 「いつ」 refers to the usual, so 「いつにもない」 is "not found at any usual time" → "unusual for you"; 「心」 is one's true feelings, so 「心にもない」 is "(words) not in one's heart" → "insincere". Turning 「ない」 into the continuative 「なく」 lets it modify the following action (「柄にもなく緊張する」).

similar.title: 〜らしい（典型・ふさわしい）
similar.explanation: 「彼らしくない」 also means "not like him" and is close in meaning, an objective evaluation of a state; 「柄にもなく」 is often self-deprecating and modifies a specific action that follows (「柄にもなく緊張した」).

similar.title: 〜にしては
similar.explanation: Both mean "differing from the usual picture". 「にしては」 can follow various nouns and verbs, meaning "for a ... (unexpectedly)"; 「にもなく」 is limited to fixed collocations such as 「柄」「いつ」「心」.

similar.title: 〜わりに
similar.explanation: Similar: both mean out of proportion to a standard. 「わりに」 is a gap against a standard like age or price; 「柄にもなく」 stresses behavior unbefitting the person's own character or position.

meaning: Repeating the same word: "even if it happens, there's another problem (or it's fine anyway)."
connection: verb た-form + ら + same verb た-form + で／verb or adjective ば-form + same word + で

senses.label: Trouble either way
senses.meaning: Something you hoped for or feared happens, and then a different problem comes up. The speaker feels nothing is ever perfect. Often resigned.
senses.connection: verb た-form + ら + same verb た-form + で
examples: Raising kids was hard when they were little, but once they grow up, there are other worries.
Not having money is a problem, but when you do have it, you end up spending it.
No rain is a problem, but when it does rain, the laundry won't dry.

senses.label: ば〜で form
senses.meaning: Same meaning as 「たら〜たで」, using the conditional 「〜ば」. Adjectives often use this form, as in 「暑ければ暑いで」.
senses.connection: verb / i-adjective ば-form + same word (た-form / dictionary form) + で
examples: When summer is hot, people complain about the heat.
Being busy at work is tiring, and having nothing to do is boring.

senses.label: It'll be fine either way
senses.meaning: When followed by something positive, it means "even then, things will work out," with an easygoing, accepting tone.
senses.connection: なければないで／なかったらなかったで + なんとかなる etc.
examples: Even without a car, you somehow manage.
If you fail, you fail. Just try again.

notes: Both halves must be the same word: ✕「降ったら止んだで」→ ○「降ったら降ったで」. Nouns and な-adjectives can't take 「たら〜たで」 directly: ✕「暇たら暇たで」→ ○「暇なら暇で」「暇だったら暇だったで」.

The second half decides the meaning: with something negative it means "even if it happens, there's trouble"; with 「なんとかなる」 or 「それでいい」 it means "even if it happens, that's fine". Reading only the first half gets it backwards.
Saying of someone 「安ければ安いで文句を言う」 criticizes them for never being satisfied, and is very rude to say to a client or boss.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Neighbors complain about the weather.
daily.example: The cold is unpleasant, but when it's hot, that's tough too.

daily.title: Talking about parenting
daily.description: Moms chat about worries after their kids start school.
daily.example: Once they start school, helping with homework is a whole new struggle.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend is worried about failing an exam.
daily.example: If you fail, you fail. You can just take it again next year.

work.title: Talking about workload
work.description: Coworkers complain about work.
work.example: When there's little work I get anxious, and when it piles up, it's overtime every day.

work.title: Project discussion
work.description: A manager shrugs off a budget problem.
work.example: If we don't get the budget, then let's think of another approach.

etymology: Made of a conditional 「〜たら／〜ば」 plus 「で」, which marks a state or cause. Repeating the word means "once it becomes that way, then in that state ...".
formation: It is formed from a conditional 「〜たら／ば」 + the same word repeated + 「で」. The first half, 「降ったら」, supposes a situation holds; the second, 「降ったで」, accepts "it rained" as an established state, and the 「で」 is generally thought to be the 「で」 of state or manner. Repeating the same word literally says "if it really becomes so, then (we face it) in that state", which naturally leads to "that has its own troubles" or "that has its own way out". The conditional of nouns and な-adjectives is 「なら」, hence 「〜なら〜で」.

similar.title: 〜わ〜わで
similar.explanation: Similar: both have a groaning "what a mess" tone and both end in 「で」. 「わ〜わで」 lists different things happening one after another (「雨は降るわ、財布はなくすわで」); this pattern is about a single event, "it has its own trouble when it happens".

similar.title: 〜たはいいが
similar.explanation: Similar: both say "it came about, but that brings other problems". 「たはいいが」 is for a specific event that has already occurred; this pattern is often a general remark and can also mean "that's fine too".

meaning: Your effort paid off and was worth it. The negative form means the effort was in vain.
connection: verb た-form／noun + の + かいがある／かいもなく

senses.label: Worth it
senses.meaning: The effort brought the result you hoped for. Often with 「努力」, 「練習」, 「待つ」. 「〜かいあって」 drops 「が」 and is more formal.
senses.connection: verb た-form + かいがある／かいがあった; noun + の + かいあって
examples: All that daily practice paid off: we won the game.
My hard work paid off, and I got into my first-choice school.
Getting up early to line up was worth it.

senses.label: In vain
senses.meaning: 「〜かいもなく」 means despite the effort, things didn't turn out as hoped. Mostly for sad results, such as a patient dying or losing a match. Fairly formal.
senses.connection: verb た-form／noun + の + かいもなく; 〜かいがない
examples: Despite his family's devoted care, my grandfather passed away.
After working this hard, if there are no results, it was all for nothing.

notes: After 「かいもなく」 must come an unwelcome result, never a good one: ✕「看病のかいもなく、元気になった」→ ○「看病のかいあって、元気になった」. Misuse gives the opposite meaning.
Saying 「頑張ったかいがなかったね」 to someone means their effort was wasted and is very hurtful; to console, avoid it and say 「残念だったけど、頑張ったことは無駄じゃないよ」.
Verbs take the た-form, not the dictionary form: ✕「練習するかいがあった」→ ○「練習したかいがあった」; nouns need 「の」: ○「努力のかいあって」.
「年甲斐もなく」 means "at your age, shamelessly ..." and has nothing to do with "no effect"; saying it to an elder is rude.

daily.title: On a trip
daily.description: Reaching the summit and seeing the view.
daily.example: Wow, it's beautiful! The climb was worth it.

daily.title: Waiting in line to eat
daily.description: Finally eating after a long wait.
daily.example: We waited an hour, but it was worth it. It was amazing.

daily.title: A sick pet
daily.description: Telling a friend about a pet's death.
daily.example: Despite the treatment, our dog died.

work.title: A successful project
work.description: A manager praises the team.
work.example: All your late nights paid off: we won the contract.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on a search-and-rescue operation.
work.example: Despite an all-out search, the man was found dead.

etymology: 「かい」 is written 「甲斐」 and originally means "effect, value, reward." The kanji 「甲斐」 are borrowed for their sound (the same as the old province 「甲斐国」) and have nothing to do with the meaning.
formation: At its core is the noun 「かい（甲斐）」, meaning "effect, reward, worth". Modified by a た-form verb or 「noun + の」, it means "the reward gained by having done ..."; followed by 「がある」 it is "the reward exists" → "it wasn't in vain, it was worth it", and followed by 「もなく」 it is "not even a reward" → "in vain", with 「も」 bringing out the regret of "despite the effort". Because a "reward" can only be for something already done, the verb must be in the た-form (「練習したかい」). 「かいあって」 is a written form dropping 「が」, linking to the next clause with the て-form.

similar.title: 〜がい（甲斐）
similar.explanation: Same origin (both 「甲斐」). 「がい」 attaches to the verb ます-stem to form compound nouns (「やりがい」「生きがい」), meaning the significance of doing something; 「かいがある」 concerns specific effort already made and says "it wasn't wasted".

similar.title: 〜だけのことはある
similar.explanation: Similar: both can mean "worth it, not in vain". 「苦労しただけのことはある」 stresses "the result matches the effort"; 「かいがある」 says more directly that "effort has paid off". 「だけのことはある」 is also often used for "as one would expect of ...".

similar.title: 〜にもかかわらず
similar.explanation: Corresponds to 「かいもなく」: both mean "in spite of ..., yet ...". 「にもかかわらず」 is an ordinary concession where anything can fill either side; 「かいもなく」 requires effort made to obtain a result before it, and a failed outcome after.

meaning: "Not to mention ..., (even) ..."; first gives an obvious case, then a broader one.
connection: noun + は言うに及ばず、noun + も／まで

senses.label: Not to mention ...
senses.meaning: Gives an obvious example first, then adds a further one. The second half often uses 「も」, 「まで」 or 「さえ」. Written style, common in news and speeches.
senses.connection: noun + は言うに及ばず、〜も／〜まで
examples: This shop is crowded on weekdays, not to mention weekends.
His novels are highly praised abroad, not to mention at home.
Even adults got hooked, to say nothing of the children.

senses.label: Needless to say
senses.meaning: Used alone as 「言うに及ばない」 or 「言うに及ばず」, it means "it goes without saying." Formal tone.
senses.connection: 〜ことは言うに及ばない; 言うに及ばず、〜
examples: It goes without saying that safety is the top priority.

notes: Put the obvious, lesser item first and the further-reaching one after it; the order can't be reversed: ✕「海外は言うに及ばず、国内でも人気だ」→ ○「国内は言うに及ばず、海外でも人気だ」.
The second half must echo with 「も」, 「まで」 or 「さえ」: ✕「週末は言うに及ばず、平日は混んでいる」→ ○「平日も混んでいる」.
It looks like 「〜には及ばない」 but differs greatly: 「ご心配には及びません」 means "there's no need to worry" and 「彼には及ばない」 means "I can't match him"; neither means "needless to say".
It is written language and sounds stiff in everyday conversation, where 「〜はもちろん」 is used. It is mostly for affirmative statements; for "let alone ... not even ..." negatives, use 「〜はおろか」.

daily.title: Recommending a place
daily.description: Recommending Kyoto to a friend.
daily.example: Kyoto's autumn leaves are stunning too, not to mention the spring cherry blossoms.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A report on a new game craze.
daily.example: They say this game is popular with older people, not to mention young people.

work.title: Product presentation
work.description: Presenting a product's strengths to a client.
work.example: This product is highly rated for its design, not to mention its performance.

work.title: Giving a speech
work.description: The president speaks at the year-end party.
work.example: I extend my heartfelt thanks to all our employees and, of course, to your families as well.

etymology: 「及ぶ」 means "to reach, to be necessary." 「言うに及ばず」 means "it doesn't even need to be said." 「ず」 is a classical negative auxiliary, which gives it a formal, dignified tone.
formation: It is built from 「言う」 + 「に」 (purpose, extent) + the literary negative 「及ばず」 of 「及ぶ」 (to reach, to be needed). 「言うに及ばない」 literally means "it hasn't reached the point of needing to be said" → "needless to say". With 「Nは」 making N the topic, it means "as for N, needless to say (that's so)", and 「〜も」 or 「〜まで」 then brings in a further example, forming a progression. 「ず」 is the literary negative auxiliary and, like 「〜なく」, can pause to link to the next clause, which also gives the whole expression a written, formal color; used alone at the end of a sentence it becomes 「言うに及ばない」.

similar.title: 〜は言うまでもなく
similar.explanation: Nearly identical in meaning. 「言うまでもなく」 is the most common and works in writing and speech; 「言うに及ばず」 uses the literary negative 「ず」 and is more formal and solemn.

similar.title: 〜は言わずもがな
similar.explanation: Similar, and equally written. 「言わずもがな」 derives from the old sense "better left unsaid" and sounds more archaic; 「言うに及ばず」 is more common in news and speeches.

similar.title: 〜はもとより・〜はもちろん
similar.explanation: Similar: both mean "... goes without saying". 「はもちろん」 is the most colloquial, 「はもとより」 more formal; 「言うに及ばず」 is the most solemn.

similar.title: 〜には及ばない
similar.explanation: Same origin, both from 「及ぶ」. 「には及ばない」 means "there's no need to ..." (「ご心配には及びません」) or "can't match ..."; this pattern is the progression "... needless to say, even ...".
